passage: Divyansh, you look worried about the loud news at dinner. Sit. I'm your Mama Mohit, and I'll tell you what happened to me at your age. It was election time. My father and my uncle shouted across the table about leaders, so angrily that I stopped eating. I thought, they both say they love this country, so why are they shouting? I went red and kept quiet. The next day I asked my father, softly, what he was most worried about. He told me. Then I asked my uncle the same. They had different answers, and both were really thinking about the country.

qa.q: What season was it when Mohit's father and uncle shouted about leaders?
What was young Mohit feeling when the elders shouted at the table?
qa.a: He was confused: both men said they loved the country, yet they shouted, and he went red and stopped eating.

qa.q: How could a child respond when elders argue about leaders?
qa.a: Listen, and ask calm questions later, as Mohit did by asking each of them what they were most worried about.

qa.q: How might Divyansh feel hearing this story from Mama Mohit?
qa.a: Probably reassured, since even Mama was confused as a child, and Divyansh learns that people can disagree and both still care about the country.

grounding: Illustrates a child confused by elders' angry arguments who asks calm questions and learns disagreement can coexist with love for the country.
